units.title: The Cold War
units.intro: Not a direct US–USSR shooting war. It was a global contest of systems: capitalism + liberal democracy vs communism + one-party state, fought with alliances, aid, spies, local wars, the arms race and the space race.

lessons.title: Development of the cold war

cards.title: 1.1 Development of the cold war
body: The longstanding distrust and suspicions, which had been building up between the Soviet Union and the West (America, Britain, France and their allies) started to resurface even before the total victory of the allies.
One immediate issue of contention between the Soviet Union and the West was the fate of Eastern Europe.
The Western powers, which had once believed that the Soviets were in a weak position, were now faced with the reality of a strong Soviet army taking possession of Eastern and much of Central Europe.
The United States demanded popular elections throughout Eastern Europe.
Unit 1 The Cold War experience in the Second World War and having lost more people than any other country in the war, the Soviet Union sought absolute military security.

cards.title: Europe split first. Berlin sat inside the Soviet zone — and was itself split.
How it started
body:
- 1945: WWII ends; wartime allies already disagree over Eastern Europe. Stalin keeps the Red Army there and installs friendly governments.
- 1947 **Truman Doctrine**: US money to states threatened by communist expansion (starts with Greece after Britain pulls out).
- 1947 **Marshall Plan**: ~＄13 billion to rebuild Western Europe so poverty would not feed revolution. USSR answers with **COMECON** (little cash behind it).
- US policy name: **containment** — hold communism where it already is.

cards.title: Model answer: how the Cold War began
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes of the Cold War after the Second World War.

steps.text: Long-term cause: distrust and suspicion between the Soviet Union and the West (America, Britain, France) that resurfaced even before the allies' final victory.
Immediate issue: the fate of Eastern Europe – the Red Army stayed there and Stalin installed friendly governments, while the USA demanded popular elections.
The Soviet view: having lost more people than any other country, the USSR sought absolute military security.

The US answer (1947): the Truman Doctrine (money to states threatened by communist expansion, starting with Greece) and the Marshall Plan (about $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe); the USSR answered with COMECON.
Name the policy: containment – hold communism where it already is.

cards.answer: Mutual distrust plus the quarrel over Eastern Europe led to rival policies – Soviet security buffer vs US containment (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan) – which split Europe into two blocs.

lessons.title: The Spread of the Cold War

cards.title: 1.2 The Spread of the Cold War
body: Soon, the United States and the Soviet Union were involved in a growing arms race, in which both countries built up their armies and weapons.
The search for security during the Cold War led to the formation of new military alliances.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was formed in April 1949 when Belgium, Luxembourg, France, the Netherlands, Great Britain, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, and Iceland signed a treaty with the United States and Canada.
All these powers agreed to provide military support if any one of them was attacked.
New military alliances spread to the rest of the world after the United States became involved in the Korean War (see next unit).

body: NATO in the west. Warsaw Pact in the east. Arms race: A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles.

body: North (backed by USSR/China) vs South (UN/US). Ends near the 38th parallel. UN action happened while the USSR was boycotting the Security Council.

cards.title: Cuba 1962

cards.title: Vietnam
body: Domino theory: if one state falls, neighbours follow. Long US war, huge anti-war movement at home, communist victory in 1975.

cards.title: Suez 1956
body: Nasser nationalises the canal. Britain, France, Israel attack; US and USSR both pressure them to stop. Nasser’s prestige rises. United Arab Republic with Syria is short-lived (Syria leaves 1961).

body: **Non-Aligned Movement:** newly independent states (Nehru, Nasser, Tito, later many Africans) refuse to be a US or Soviet satellite.
**UN:** born 1945 to keep peace. Cold War often froze the Security Council with vetoes. Still a stage for debate, agencies and rare joint action.

cards.title: Model answer: the Cuban Missile Crisis
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why is the Cuban Missile Crisis seen as the most dangerous moment of the Cold War, and how was it solved?

steps.text: What happened: the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles on the island of Cuba, close to the USA.
Why dangerous: it was the closest brush with nuclear war in the arms race (A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles).
The deal: Soviet missiles were taken out of Cuba; later US missiles were taken out of Turkey; the USA promised not to invade Cuba.
Link to the theme: it shows how the arms race spread the Cold War beyond Europe.

cards.answer: Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers to the edge of nuclear war; it ended with a deal – missiles out of Cuba, later US missiles out of Turkey and a US promise not to invade Cuba.

lessons.title: United Nations Organization and the Cold war

cards.title: 1.3 United Nations Organization and the Cold war
body: The United Nations Organization (UNO) was established immediately after the end of the Second World War.
The founders of the UN believed that future disputes between countries could be settled by discussion, conciliation and arbitration.
Member states could be called upon to make troops available for peacekeeping missions.
Representatives of all states belonging to the UN meet at least once a year in New York for the General Assembly.
The five permanent members of the Security Council (the USA, USSR, Britain, France and China) have a privileged position compared to other member states.

cards.title: Model answer: the UN and the Cold War
cards.problem: (Short answer) Explain how the United Nations was organised to keep peace and why the Cold War limited it.

steps.text: Founding idea: the UN was set up right after the Second World War; its founders believed disputes could be settled by discussion, conciliation and arbitration.
General Assembly: all member states meet at least once a year in New York.
Security Council: five permanent members (USA, USSR, Britain, France, China) have a privileged position; member states can be asked to provide troops for peacekeeping.
Cold War limit: the two rival superpowers both sat as permanent members, so they could block each other (in Korea the UN acted only because the USSR was boycotting the Security Council).

cards.answer: The UN works through the General Assembly and the Security Council, but superpower rivalry among the permanent five often paralysed it during the Cold War.

To create a new industrial base, therefore, Stalin returned to the method that he had used in the 1930s.
Soviet workers were expected to produce goods for export with little reward.
The incoming capital from abroad could then be used to buy machinery and Western technology.
Economic recovery in the Soviet Union was spectacular.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Compare domestic developments in the Eastern and Western blocs after 1945.

steps.text: East – recovery: the USSR (25 million dead) rebuilt with Stalin's 1930s methods: exports with little reward for workers, capital spent on Western machinery – spectacular recovery.

cards.title: 1.5 From Cold War to Post-Cold War
body: By the 1970s, American-Soviet relations had entered a new phase, known as détente, which was marked by a relaxation of tensions and improved relations between the two superpowers.
Beginning in 1979, however, the apparent collapse of détente began a new period of East-West confrontation.
The American-Soviet détente faced a major setback in 1979, when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan.
The Soviet Union intended to support a client regime in Afghanistan, which the United States viewed as an act of expansion.
America placed an embargo on the shipment of American grain to the Soviets.

tips.text: The world from just the end of the Second World War up to 1990 was dominated by what was called the 'Cold War’.
Unlike the active conflict of the Second World War, the Cold War was a long period of tension and hostility that only occasionally broke out into open warfare.
This tension was caused by rivalry between the two superpowers that emerged after the end of the Second World War— the United States and the Soviet Union.
Underlying this rivalry were the ideological divisions between the two superpowers.
The United States was a capitalist liberal democracy.
The Soviet Union, on the other hand, was a oneparty socialist state. Each power tried to influence other nations to support its own way of life.
After 1945, a division emerged between the capitalist West (the US and Western Europe); and the socialist states (the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, and after 1949, China).
Both the US and the Soviet Union tried to influence the newly independent states in Africa and Asia.
On several occasions this caused open conflicts.
The prominent examples of such conflicts were Vietnam War (1960-75) and Angolan Civil War (1975-79).

body: At the end of World War II, British India’s Muslims and Hindus were bitterly divided.
The British decided to divide India into two countries, one majority Hindu (India) and the other Muslim (Pakistan).

One part, West Pakistan, was to the northwest of India.

cards.title: 3.1 Factors that led to independence in Africa
body: For most African countries, the process was a peaceful one.
Independence came as a result of negotiations between the colonial power and representatives from the colony.

In contrast, in the colonies with large numbers of European settlers (such as Algeria, Kenya and Zimbabwe), the process involved lengthy wars of liberation before the colonial powers were forced to accept majority rule.
The world wars drained the economies of the European colonial powers.
The colonial powers also realized that they did not have to keep political power to maintain economic influence in their former colonies.

cards.title: Model answer: why Africa became independent
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the factors that led to independence in Africa after 1945.

steps.text: Weakened Europe: the world wars drained the economies of the European colonial powers.
Changed thinking: the powers realised they did not need political power to keep economic influence in their former colonies.
Path 1 – negotiation: for most African countries independence came peacefully through negotiations between the colonial power and representatives of the colony.
Path 2 – war: in settler colonies (Algeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe) lengthy wars of liberation were needed before majority rule was accepted.

cards.answer: Exhausted colonial economies and the belief that economic influence could continue without rule led to independence – mostly negotiated, but won by long wars where European settlers were numerous.

lessons.title: Decolonization in British Colonies

cards.title: 3.2 Decolonization in British Colonies
body: Ghana, and Nkrumah, became an inspiration to other nationalist movements in Africa.
A year before, in 1956, the Sudan gained its independence from the British.
Beginning from 1899 Sudan was formally under AngloEgyptian rule where it was run by a governor-general appointed by Egypt with British consent.
In reality, Sudan was effectively a British colony.
In 1954 Egypt gave up its claims to authority in the Sudan, a claim which dated back to the precolonial conquest of Mohammed Ali.

cards.title: Colonial power shaped the exit. Portuguese and settler regimes fought longest.
Decolonization in British Colonies
body:
- **British:** often staged constitutions. Model case: Gold Coast / Ghana under Nkrumah (1957), then a wave in the 1960s. Kenya includes Mau Mau; settler politics complicate it.
- **French:** at first “French Union / Community”; Guinea says no in 1958. Algeria: long, bitter war until 1962.
- **Belgian Congo:** sudden 1960 independence, almost no preparation, then crisis and foreign meddling.
- **Portuguese:** Lisbon treats colonies as provinces; armed struggle in Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau until the 1974 Lisbon coup.
- **Italian:** Libya earlier; Horn trusteeships (including the UN path that affected Eritrea — the book treats the national struggle in Unit 5).
- **Southern Africa:** apartheid South Africa, UDI Rhodesia, Portuguese neighbours — freedom delayed into the 1970s–90s (Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990, democratic SA 1994).

cards.problem: (Short answer) Describe how Britain decolonised its African colonies, with examples.

steps.text: Method: Britain often staged constitutions – step-by-step transfer of power.
Model case: the Gold Coast became Ghana under Nkrumah in 1957 (Sudan in 1956 even earlier); then a wave of independence in the 1960s.

Southern Africa: freedom was delayed – Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990, democratic South Africa 1994.

cards.answer: Britain mostly transferred power step by step through constitutions (Sudan 1956, Ghana 1957, then many in the 1960s), but settler colonies took longer.

lessons.title: Decolonization in French colonies

cards.title: 3.3 Decolonization in French colonies
body: In 1958, France offered its colonies in French West Africa and French Equatorial Africa the choice of becoming independent countries within the French Community (with economic aid from France) or fully independent.
In the French Community, each state would run its own internal affairs, but would send representatives to a central council in Paris which would control foreign policy and defense.
Only Guinea chose full independence and cut all ties with France.
When Guinea opted for full independence instead of joining the French Community, France decided to teach it a lesson.
France tried to cripple the new state, by withdrawing all aid, personnel and equipment.

**Step 2:** **Step 1:** Recall the 1958 French Constitutional Referendum proposed by Charles de Gaulle.
**Step 2:** French colonies were given a choice: join the 'French Community' (limited autonomy) or take immediate independence (cutting all ties with France).
**Step 3:** **Guinea**, led by Ahmed Sékou Touré, was the only colony to vote 'No' to the community and choose immediate independence.
**Result:** Guinea.

**Step 3:** So the answer is B) Guinea.

cards.answer: The Community offered self-rule under Paris's control of foreign policy and defence; only Guinea chose full independence and was punished by France's withdrawal of all aid.

cards.title: 3.4 Decolonization in Belgian colonies
body: The transfer of power took place more suddenly in the Belgian Congo than anywhere else.
Initially Belgium wanted a 30-year period to prepare her colony for independence.
In the other Belgian colonies - Rwanda and Burundi - the legacy of Belgian rule resulted in civil war and genocide.
In both territories, the Belgians had used the minority Tutsi in the administration to control the majority Hutu.
After independence, deep-seated ill-feelings between the two groups got worse.

cards.answer: Sudden independence without preparation (Congo 1960) and divide-and-rule between Tutsi and Hutu (Rwanda, Burundi) left crisis, civil war and genocide.

cards.title: 3.5 Decolonization in Portuguese colonies
body: By the 1970s these wars were costing almost half the Portuguese budget and involving increasing numbers of troops.
In 1974, army officers in Portugal, who were determined to end the futile colonial wars, overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal.
The new government quickly granted independence to the three colonies.
Mozambique, Samora Machel, the leader of FRELIMO (Front for the Liberation of Mozambique), became the first president.

The situation in Angola was complicated by the existence of three rival resistance groups, superpower backing the two rival groups, and the involvement of Apartheid South Africa and Cuba (See next unit).

steps.text: Portugal's view: Lisbon treated its colonies as provinces and refused to leave.

cards.answer: Portugal held on until armed struggle made the wars unbearably costly; the 1974 Lisbon coup then brought quick independence to Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.

Ethiopia saw the period of decolonization as an ideal opportunity to gain an outlet to the sea.
At the United Nations, powerful states especially the USA favored Ethiopian claims.
The UN therefore denied Eritreans their right to self-determination and, preferring to hand Eritrea to Ethiopia in 1952 by way of an unviable federation.

cards.answer: Ethiopia's wish for a sea outlet, backed by the USA at the UN, led to the 1952 federation that denied Eritreans the independence most of them wanted.

body: Not surprisingly, in South Africa, the country with the largest population of white settlers, resistance to African majority rule had been strong.

African majority rule in South Africa would have to be achieved through the struggles of the majority of South Africans.
In 1948 a National Party, a party of Afrikaner supremacist won an overall majority in the whites-only general election.

lessons.title: Organization of African Unity

cards.title: 3.8 Organization of African Unity
body: In the early 1960s, as more African states became independent, there was growing support for African unity, which was one of the ideals of Pan-Africanism (see grade 11 textbook).
The Casablanca bloc, led by Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, wanted a federation of all African countries.
The group included Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali and Libya.
The Monrovian bloc, led by Senghor of Senegal, felt that unity should be achieved gradually, through economic cooperation.
The differences of opinion were resolved when the emperor of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie, invited both groups to a meeting in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia.

cards.title: Organization of African Unity
body: **OAU (1963, Addis Ababa):** African unity, respect for inherited borders (to avoid border wars), support for remaining liberation movements. Ancestor of today’s AU.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The differences of opinion were resolved when the emperor of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie, invited both groups to a meeting in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia.”

**Step 2:** Before the OAU was formed, African leaders were divided into two groups: The **Monrovia Group** (moderate, including **Ethiopia**, Nigeria, and Liberia) and the Casablanca Group (radical, including Ghana, Egypt, and Mali).

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) Ethiopia.

**Step 2:** Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana was the most vocal advocate for the immediate political and economic unification of Africa (the 'United States of Africa'). He believed that individual African states were too weak to survive alone against neo-colonialism.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Kwame Nkrumah.

**Step 2:** South Africa was not allowed to join the OAU in 1963 because of its institutionalized system of racial segregation known as **Apartheid**. The OAU's primary goal was to end colonialism and white minority rule in Africa.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) South Africa.

cards.title: Model answer: founding of the OAU
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the OAU was formed in 1963 and what its aims were.

steps.text: Background: as more states became independent in the early 1960s, support grew for African unity, an ideal of Pan-Africanism.

Two blocs: the Casablanca bloc (Nkrumah of Ghana; Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali, Libya) wanted a federation of all Africa; the Monrovian bloc (Senghor of Senegal) wanted gradual unity through economic cooperation.
Compromise: Emperor Haile Selassie invited both groups to Addis Ababa, and the OAU was founded there in 1963.
Aims: African unity, respect for inherited borders (to avoid border wars) and support for remaining liberation movements.

cards.answer: The OAU (Addis Ababa, 1963) was a compromise between the Casablanca and Monrovian blocs, aiming at unity, respect for colonial borders and support for liberation movements.

tips.text: Decolonization in Africa in the 1960s and 1970s was mainly a result of nationalist movements that emerged in most African countries after the Second World War.
Other factors that contributed for African independence include: the weakening of colonial powers after the WWII and Cold War politics.
The British and French granted independence to their colonies in the 1950s and 1960s, mainly peacefully.
Problems arose where there were settlers of European descent, and there were major conflicts in areas such as Kenya, Algeria and Zimbabwe.
Belgium, though reluctant at first, also granted independence to its colonies in the 1960s.
The Portuguese were less willing to give up their colonies, and long wars of liberation took place in Angola and Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique, which lasted until the mid1970s.
One of the major post-independence developments in Africa was the creation of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) in 1963.
The Organization of African Unity was made up of all independent states that supported the charter.
In 2002, the OAU was replaced by the African Union.

body: The leaders of the nationalist movements at the time of independence had great hopes for their new states.
Free from foreign control, the new governments, run by Africans, would make decisions for the new nations.
The ideal of African nationalists, that Africa should decide its own destiny, seemed now to have come true.
Two of the most immediate goals of the newly independent states in Africa were promoting economic growth and ensuring national unity.
The new African leaders were optimistic that freedom from colonial control would result in economic prosperity.

cards.title: 4.3 Challenges of Independence: Colonial legacies
body: Most historians agree that the colonial legacy was the underlying cause of many of these challenges.
Many historians believe that part of the explanation for this lies in the period of colonial rule, which by its very nature is oppressive and dictatorial.
The colonial authorities had kept control by using force and silencing any criticism or opposition.
After independence, many African leaders, who had themselves been prisoners of the colonial authorities, used the same methods.
By the late 1960s, many independent African countries were one-party states where opposition parties were banned and their leaders jailed.

cards.title: 4.5 Africa after the Cold War
body: Since 1990 most of Africa has seen political changes, as military dictatorships and one-party states have given way to multi-party systems.

Africa was no longer the playing field for influence by rival superpowers.

Corrupt and ineffective governments or long-standing dictators, such as Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire were no longer supported with external funds or arms supplies simply because they declared themselves to be anticommunist or anti-capitalist.

tips.text: Once free from colonial rule, African countries pursued different polcies to construct new societies. Some, like Kenya, followed a capitalist path, while others, like Tanzania pursued socialist policies.
Independence brought opportunities and possibilities for the new states. But there were also many challenges facing them.
Ethnic conflicts broke out, such as the Biafran War in Nigeria.
Political instability led to military coups in several states, such as that of Idi Amin in Uganda.
The legacy of colonialism also left them without a balanced economy and dependent on foreign markets.
Problems such as drought, disease, high population growth rates and poverty created major difficulties as well.

The newly independent African states thus faced problems which placed them at a disadvantage in comparison to many other countries. So the hopes that independence would bring peace and prosperity to Africa were unrealized by the end of the 1970s.

The after-effects of colonialism meant that African states were particularly vulnerable to internal conflicts, and this was made worse by the impact of international economic and political factors during the Cold War.
State types: Some tried liberal constitutions, many moved to one-party or military rule “for unity”. Ideals (unity, development, dignity) collided with weak institutions.

Colonial legacy: Borders that cut nations and join rivals; economies built to export one crop or mineral; few industries; schools and civil service too small; capital cities favoured over the countryside.
Internal + external: Ethnic and regional tension, coups, debt. Cold War patrons armed clients. After 1990, fewer superpower cheques, more talk of multiparty politics and structural adjustment.

lessons.title: The Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) and the early years of the Armed Struggle

cards.title: 5.1 The Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) and the early years of the Armed Struggle
body: With the rise of Gamal Abdel Nasser to power, Egypt was providing generous admission to students from Africa and the Middle East to its secondary and higher education institutions.
With the increasing opposition to Ethiopian polices in 1950s, the number of students going to Egypt increased.
Cairo of that time was a center of intense revolutionary activities, where radical movements from Africa and the Middle East were freely operating.

With the process of the dismantlement of the federation proceeding relentlessly and the growing suppression of the Ethiopian government of all nationalists, some Eritrean leaders went to Egypt as political exiles.
Prominent among them were Weldeab Weldemariam, Ibrahim Sultan and Idris Mohammed Adem.

**Step 2:** The ELF (Jebha) was formally founded in July 1960 in **Cairo**, Egypt, by a group of Eritrean exiles including Idris Mohammed Adem.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the ELF was founded and how the armed struggle began.

steps.text: Background: the federation was being dismantled and Ethiopia suppressed nationalists, so leaders such as Weldeab Weldemariam, Ibrahim Sultan and Idris Mohammed Adem went to Egypt as exiles; Nasser's Cairo was a centre of revolutionary movements and hosted many Eritrean students.
Founding: in July 1960 Idris Mohammed Adem and Eritrean students founded the ELF in Cairo with the aim of liberating Eritrea by armed struggle.
First shot: Hamid Idris Awate opened the armed struggle on 1 September 1961 near Mount Adal.
Early growth: operations such as Hykota (1963) and Togorba (1964); the Cairo-based Supreme Council led the organisation.

cards.answer: Exiles and students in Nasser's Cairo founded the ELF in July 1960, and Awate's first shot at Mount Adal on 1 September 1961 began the armed struggle.

lessons.title: The period of Zonal Commands (1965-1968)

cards.title: 5.2 The period of Zonal Commands (1965-1968)
body: In the history of the Eritrean Armed Struggle what is referred to as the “period of zonal/regional commands” is the time when the ELA was divided into 5 separate zonal/regional commands that had a clearly designated operational zone.
On July 20, 1965, the Supreme Council, together with representatives that came from inside the field and other countries, held a meeting in Kassala, Eastern Sudan.
The establishment of the zonal/regional commands was taken from the experience of the Algerian Revolution.
The Kassala meeting divided the ELA into 4 zonal commands and, as the number of Tigrigna-speaking fighters grew, a 5th zonal command was added in 1966 to accommodate them.
Seid Adem was appointed as the head of the Revolutionary Command.

cards.why:

**Step 2:** **Step 1:** List the dates of the events.
- Zonal Commands (ELF): Established in **1965**.
- Adobha Conference: Held in **1969**.
- Formation of EPLF: Emerged in the early **1970s**.
- The Rectification Movement (Islah): **1987**.
- Fenkil Operation: **1990**.
**Result:** Zonal commands were established first.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Establishment of zonal commands.

**Step 2:** In 1965, the ELF divided Eritrea into five military zones. This system led to tribalism and inefficiency. During the **Adobha Conference (1969)**, the zones were abolished and replaced by a unified **General Command** (*Al-Qiyada Al-Ama*).

cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the period of zonal commands (1965–1968) in the ELF.

steps.text: Decision: on 20 July 1965 the Supreme Council and field representatives met in Kassala, eastern Sudan.
Model: the idea came from the Algerian Revolution.
Structure: the ELA was divided into 4 zonal commands, with a 5th added in 1966 for the growing number of Tigrinya-speaking fighters; Seid Adem headed a Kassala-based Revolutionary Command.
End: the system caused division, and the Adobha Conference (1969) abolished the zones and formed a united General Command.

cards.answer: From 1965 the ELA fought in separate zones on the Algerian model (4 zones, then 5 in 1966) until the Adobha Conference of 1969 replaced them with a united command.

steps.text: Three groups split from the ELF: the first, whose Imba Hara conference (1971) elected a leadership chaired by Romadan Mohammed Nur; the second (the Alla group, leadership chaired by Isaias Afwerki, document "We and Our Goals"); the third, the Eritrean Liberation Forces (Ubel), named after the Ubel River meeting.
Support: Osman Saleh Sabe's General Secretariat gave logistical support because he wanted a force inside Eritrea of his own.
Merger: in February 1972 the groups and Sabe's General Secretariat met to form the Eritrean People's Liberation Forces.
Why: opposition to the undemocratic line of the ELF General Command and to sectarian divisions.

cards.answer: Three groups that left the ELF, backed by Osman Saleh Sabe's General Secretariat, united in 1972 as the Eritrean People's Liberation Forces, rejecting the General Command's undemocratic and divisive line.

lessons.title: Eritrean War of Independence and the fall of the Haile Sellasie Regime

cards.title: 5.4 Eritrean War of Independence and the fall of the Haile Sellasie Regime
body: After a few months of turmoil and instability, Emperor Haile Sellasie was officially deposed on 11 September 1974 and Ethiopia fell under the control of a military regime that called itself the Provisional Military Council, or the Derg.
Along with the economic crisis and public uprising in Ethiopia, the Eritrean Revolution was a key factor that pushed the Haile Sellasie regime to its demise.
The Eritrean war of independence transitioned from a guerilla hit and run battles to mobile and conventional battles.
The Derg was paying lip-service to peaceful resolution of the Eritrean question until it completed its military preparation for a new offensive.
All over Eritrea, the Derg regime initiated an unprecedented and widespread massacres and burning of villages.

**Step 2:** During the Strategic Retreat of 1978, the Derg regime received massive military support from the Soviet Union (USSR), Cuba, and South Yemen. This support included advanced weaponry, military advisors, and combat troops, which forced the EPLF and ELF to withdraw from liberated towns.

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) All.

cards.title: Model answer: the fall of Haile Sellasie
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes of the fall of Haile Sellasie's regime in 1974 and the role of the Eritrean Revolution.

steps.text: Famine: the 1973 famine and the regime's attempt to hide it angered Ethiopians.
Economic crisis: a petrol-price rise in February 1974 led to a taxi drivers' strike, joined by students and teachers.
Eritrean factor: in December 1973 the Second Division suffered heavy casualties against the EPLF in Northern Sahel and mutinied; the mutiny spread across the army.
Result: the cabinet resigned and the emperor was deposed on 11 September 1974; the military Derg took power.

cards.answer: Famine, economic crisis and popular uprisings, together with army mutinies triggered by defeats in Eritrea, brought down the emperor on 11 September 1974.

The Congress changed the name “Eritrean People’s Liberation Forces” to “Eritrean People’s Liberation Front” and approved the design of the EPLF’s flag and emblem.
The Congress believed that the best way to achieve the goal is through establishing a United Front.

steps.text: Background: by 1976, 90% of rural Eritrea was under the Revolution; the Congress confirmed "liberating the land and people step by step".
EPLA advances: Karora (January 1977), Nakfa (March 1977, a turning point), Afabet (6 April 1977), then Dekemhare and Keren (July 1977), Segeneiti and Digsa; by the end of 1977 Asmara was encircled.
ELF advances: Omhajer, Tessenei, Adi Quala, Mendefera and Akordet.
Result: by early 1978 only Assab, Asmara, Adi Keih, Barentu and part of Massawa remained in Ethiopian hands.

cards.answer: In 1977 the EPLA and ELF liberated most towns (Karora first, Nakfa the turning point, then Afabet, Keren, Dekemhare...), leaving only Assab, Asmara, Adi Keih, Barentu and part of Massawa by early 1978.

cards.title: Model answer: socio-economic changes
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the socio-economic changes brought by the Revolution in the liberated areas.

steps.text: Land reform: within the Diessa system, the unmarried, women and non-original inhabitants gained land rights; landless peasants on the coast received land.
Health: prevention of disease, mobile teams, barefoot doctors and trained midwives; later Orotta hospital and frontline surgery.
Education: a national curriculum, village schools, adult education and the Revolution School in Sahel (Tigrinya, Arabic, Tigre); the ELF opened Tsibah School.
Women: equal rights in marriage, divorce, inheritance, land and politics; over 30% of the army by the 1980s.

cards.answer: The Revolution brought fairer land rights, preventive health care, schools and adult education, and women's equality in the liberated areas.

lessons.title: Effort for Unity between the ELF and EPLF

cards.title: 5.8 Effort for Unity between the ELF and EPLF
body: Since the Foreign Mission signed the agreement, which undermined the process which had started in the field, the EPLF rejected and condemned it in its first conference of Semenawi Bahri (7-12 November, 1975).
Accordingly, the EPLF withdrew to the mountainous Sahel region and the ELF withdrew to the western lowlands, the Barka region.
The battles of Elabered and Mamiede are two good examples where the invading Ethiopian army faced crashing defeats at the hands of the EPLF.

cards.title: Model answer: efforts for unity
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the efforts for unity between the ELF and EPLF (1975–1977).

steps.text: Start: after the civil war ended in 1974, dialogue committees were formed in March 1975; the ELF's Second Congress (May 1975) mandated dialogue.

Setback: the Foreign Mission signed the Khartoum Agreement (September 1975) behind the field; the EPLF condemned it at Semenawi Bahri (November 1975) and the Foreign Mission split off (March 1976) as ELF-PLF.
Agreement: the October 20, 1977 Unity Agreement in Khartoum.
Its points: unity through joint work programs, a joint political leadership and a joint military strategy.

cards.answer: Dialogue began in 1975, was disrupted by the Foreign Mission's Khartoum Agreement, and produced the 20 October 1977 Unity Agreement for joint leadership and joint military strategy.

cards.title: Model answer: Soviet intervention and the strategic withdrawal
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the Soviet intervention of 1977–78 and its effect on the Eritrean Revolution.

steps.text: Cause: the Derg broke with the USA (by July 1977) and turned to the Soviet Union, which allied with Ethiopia for its own interests; Mengistu visited Moscow in May 1977.
Size: $1–2 billion of arms, 12,000 Cuban troops and 1,500 advisers, plus Libyan money and South Yemeni pilots and units.
Effect: the balance tilted to the Derg and stopped a possible Eritrean victory in 1978.
Response: a strategic withdrawal – EPLF to Sahel, ELF to Barka – carried out while inflicting heavy losses (Elabered, Mamiede), so the protracted war could continue.

cards.answer: Massive Soviet-bloc aid tilted the balance to the Derg in 1978, forcing a planned strategic withdrawal to Sahel (EPLF) and Barka (ELF) to continue the protracted war.

lessons.title: The Derg’s Successive military offensives against the Eritrean Revolution

cards.title: 5.10 The Derg’s Successive military offensives against the Eritrean Revolution
body: The five consecutive military campaigns utterly failed to achieve the primary goal - defeating the Eritrean Revolution once for all.

The sixth offensive, also called the “Red Star Campaign” by the Derg, was the largest, fiercest, most multi-dimensional, and most challenging of all the previous successive offensives that aimed to destroy and annihilate the EPLF.
The Derg was also ready to go to the extent of using internationally prohibited chemical weapons.
Yet, if armaments and other resources were considered the overall military balance of power between the EPLF and the Derg was overwhelmingly in favor of the latter.

Even though the EPLF had foiled the Derg’s ultimate goal of destroying the Eritrean Revolution, the war had a heavy toll on the front. 2,700 freedom fighters were martyred, and 5,000 were lightly and heavily wounded.

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2015)
cards.q: Which Derg’s offensive known as the **“Red Star Campaign”** was?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The sixth offensive, also called the “Red Star Campaign” by the Derg, was the largest, fiercest, most multi-dimensional, and most challenging of all the previous successive offensives that aimed to destroy and annihilate the EPLF.”

**Step 2:** The **Red Star Campaign** (also known as the Sixth Offensive or 'Selahta Werar') was launched by the Derg regime in 1982. It was a massive military operation aimed at crushing the Eritrean revolution once and for all, but it ultimately failed.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Sixth.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The sixth offensive, also called the “Red Star Campaign” by the Derg, was the largest, fiercest, most multi-dimensional, and most challenging of all the previous successive offensives that aimed to destroy and annihilate the EPLF.”

**Step 2:** The **6th Offensive**, also known as the **Red Star Campaign** (*Zemecha Keyih Kokeb*), launched in 1982, was the largest and most prepared Ethiopian military campaign aimed at crushing the Eritrean revolution (EPLF) in Nakfa.

**Step 3:** So the answer is B) 6th offensive..

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

**Step 2:** The **Seventh Offensive** (also known as the 'Stealth Offensive' or 'Silent Offensive') was launched in 1985 without the usual propaganda fanfares used in the Sixth (Red Star) offensive.

cards.title: Model answer: the Red Star Campaign
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why was the Derg's sixth offensive (Red Star Campaign) significant?

steps.text: Background: five offensives (1978–79) had failed to destroy the Eritrean Revolution.
Scale: the sixth, "Red Star Campaign", was the largest, fiercest and most multi-dimensional; the Derg spent two years preparing and was ready to use prohibited chemical weapons.
Result: the Derg was defeated and lost about 54,000 troops, though the EPLF paid heavily (2,700 martyred, 5,000 wounded).
Significance: after it and the Stealth (seventh) Offensive of 1983 failed, any hope of destroying the Revolution militarily was gone.

cards.answer: The Red Star Campaign was the Derg's biggest effort to crush the EPLF; its failure, despite heavy EPLF losses, showed the Revolution could not be destroyed militarily.

lessons.title: The Second Civil War and the Disintegration of ELF

cards.title: 5.11 The Second Civil War and the Disintegration of ELF
body: As already stated in previous lessons, the ELF had fragmented into many factions after it was forced into the Sudan.
One of these factions was the ELF Central Leadership (Sagim).

cards.title: Rule
body: Eritrea: 1961 armed start ELF then EPLF 1991 liberation

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2026)
cards.q: One of the following events did **not** occur in the 1970s.

options.C: The beginning of Soviet intervention on Derg's side
options.E: The approval of National Democratic Program by EPLF

cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “In August 1981, the ELF military units were pushed over to the Sudan, and were disarmed by the Sudanese government.”

**Step 2:** The **demise of the ELF** (following the second civil war) occurred in the early 1980s (1981), not in the 1970s.

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) The demise of ELF.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2023)
cards.q: After the death of Hamid Idris Awate the field leadership of ELF was fell under the following leaders, **except**
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “When Hamid Idris Awate died in mid-1962, the field leadership of ELF was held successively by Muhammad Idris Hajj, Muhammad Omer Abdulla (Abu Tiyara), Abu-Bakr Muhammad Idris and Mahmud Dinai.”

**Step 2:** After the death of Hamid Idris Awate in 1962, the field leadership was coordinated by a group often referred to as the **General Command** or the initial field commanders, which included Mahmud Dinai, Muhammed Idris Hajj, and others. **Abu-Bakr Muhammad Idris** was not part of this specific early transition leadership group.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Mohammed Ali Omaro..

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.q: The new leadership **Kiada -al- Amma** was product of___in 1969.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “In this conference (Adobha, 1969) a 38-member General Command was established.”

**Step 2:** The **Adobha Conference** (1969) was held to resolve internal crises within the ELF. It resulted in the dissolution of the Sector system and the creation of a temporary unified leadership called **Kiada al-Amma** (General Command).

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Adobha Conference.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Model answer: the second civil war
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the second civil war and the disintegration of the ELF.

steps.text: Hopes: in April 1978 both fronts agreed to implement the October 1977 agreement (joint political leadership and committees).
Breakdown: deep political disagreements and clashes; from mid-1980 relations worsened and in July 1980 all-out war began.
Mediation failed: the Arab League meeting in Tunis did not stop the fighting.
End: in August 1981 ELF units were pushed into the Sudan and disarmed; they split into hostile factions such as the ELF Central Leadership (Sagim) – the ELF ceased to exist as a united force.

cards.answer: Unity talks collapsed into civil war in July 1980; by August 1981 the ELF was pushed into the Sudan, disarmed and broke into factions.

cards.title: Model answer: from defence to offense
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe how the Eritrean Revolution moved from defence to offense (1984–1987).

steps.text: Stalemate: after the Red Star Campaign and the Stealth Offensive failed, the war reached stalemate; the EPLF built up its strength.
Initiatives in 1984: Tessenei and Alighedr captured (January), the Wuqaw Command routed (March, ~7,000 Derg losses), 33 planes destroyed at Asmara air base.
1985: Barentu liberated on 5 July (retaken after the Derg brought troops from the Ogaden); the eighth offensive, Bahri Negash (October 1985), failed with ~17,000 losses.
Result: increased guerrilla and commando operations meant that by the end of 1987 the war reached the stage of strategic offensive.

cards.answer: From 1984 to 1987 the EPLF broke the stalemate with major attacks (Wuqaw, Asmara air base, Barentu) and defeated the last Derg offensive, reaching the strategic offensive by 1987.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the decisions of the EPLF's Second and Unity Congress (1987).

steps.text: Name: it was the EPLF's Second Organizational Congress and a Unity Congress with the ELF Central Leadership (Sagim).
Meeting: 12–19 March 1987 with 1,287 delegates; Weldeab Weldemariam attended and Ibrahim Sultan sent a video message.

cards.answer: The 1987 congress united the EPLF with Sagim, adopted an amended National Democratic Program (pluralism, mixed economy, non-alignment) and elected Isaias Afwerki Secretary General.

lessons.title: The Strategic Offensive and Independence (1988-1991)

cards.title: Timeline
head: Date
Event
rows: — After Italian rule and British administration, Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia (1952) then annexed (1962). Political space closed; many nationalists concluded that only arms would work.
— Armed struggle begins. **ELF** (Eritrean Liberation Front) organises the early years.
— **Zonal commands**: ELF divides the field into zones. The system spreads the fight but also plants rivalry and weak central strategy.
— Reform currents and splits. **EPLF** (Eritrean People’s Liberation Front / Forces) is born and grows a different model: tighter organisation, political work among civilians, self-reliance.
— Ethiopian revolution: Haile Selassie falls, the **Derg** takes over. At first towns fall to the fronts; then the new regime, later backed by heavy **Soviet** aid, launches successive offensives.
Civil wars between ELF and EPLF
— Unity talks fail more than once. A later civil war ends with ELF forces pushed out; EPLF remains the main front inside the country.
— After surviving the Red Star and other Derg campaigns, the EPLF moves from holding the base areas to taking towns, then the **strategic offensive**.

— Ethiopian state collapses in the north; Eritrean forces take Asmara. Formal independence follows the 1993 referendum. The book also notes socio-economic work in liberated areas (schools, clinics, land, women’s participation) as part of the revolution, not only battles.

cards.title: Do not flatten 30 years into one date. Exams like the sequence: ELF → zones → EPLF → Derg/Soviet offensives → unity crisis → strategic win.
How to write a Unit 5 paragraph
body: 1) Political cause (federation/annexation). 2) Who fought first (ELF). 3) Why a second organisation appeared. 4) How the Ethiopian state changed in 1974 and why that mattered. 5) How the war ended in 1991. Add one social fact (education, women, land) if asked for “revolution” not only “war”.

cards.title: Exercise — source question style
cards.problem: A fighter’s memoir (1995) says the zonal system “destroyed unity”. A 1966 ELF leaflet says zones “brought the struggle to every province”. How do you use both?

steps.text: Both are primary-ish, but one is later memory and one is wartime propaganda.
They disagree because they have different jobs: recruit vs explain defeat.
A good answer uses both: zones did spread the fight *and* created command rivalries — which is why the textbook treats 1965–68 as its own phase.
Never quote one and pretend the other does not exist.

cards.answer: Never quote one and pretend the other does not exist.

cards.title: Model answer: the strategic offensive and independence
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the strategic offensive that led to Eritrean independence (1988–1993).

steps.text: Nadew (17–19 March 1988): the 22,000-strong Nadew Command was destroyed and Afabet liberated in 48 hours – the balance tipped to the EPLF.
Fenkil (8 February 1990): Massawa was liberated after three days – the beginning of the end of Ethiopian occupation.
Final battles: the south (Senafe, Adi Keih, Segeneiti) in 1990, Dankalia in 1991, Dekemhare in May 1991; on 24 May 1991 the EPLF entered Asmara and on 26 May Assab was liberated.
Independence: in the UN- and OAU-observed referendum of 23–25 April 1993, 99.8% voted for independence (result 27 April 1993).

cards.answer: Nadew (1988), Fenkil (1990) and the final offensive brought liberation on 24 May 1991; the 1993 referendum (99.8% yes) made Eritrea an internationally recognised state.

tips.text: In 1952 Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia on the basis of the UN Resolution 390A (V).
The federal arrangement had problems from the very beginning.
The Ethiopian government accepted it as a spring board for future annexation. It, thus, started violating the Federal Act gradually and in 1962 Ethiopia annexed Eritrea.
A year before the complete annexation of Eritrea Hamid Idris Awate on behalf of the ELF, shot the first bullet marking the beginning of the Eritrean armed struggle for independence.
The Eritrean Armed Struggle, one of the longest and most successful liberation struggles of the Twentieth century, continued for thirty years.
With the political and military failings of the ELF, dissident fighters tried to reform the Front but with little success.
In 1970 some of those fighters left ELF in different groups and later formed an alternative Front known as the EPLF.
Civil war broke out between the two Fronts consuming considerable time and energy.
The EPLF led a successful war and liberated Eritrea on 24 May 1991 by deafeating the Ethiopian army, the largest in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Eritrea: 1961 armed start ELF then EPLF 1991 liberation
